commentBody: A Tuesday Thursday. Not surprising following what others have described as three Mondays. Oh well; there should be lots of "Fastest Thursday ever" posts. Nice grid, Jeff, but the clues...
Cute! And a new personal best, hooray.

Number one rule at the crossword club:

Any rule can be broken in the service of a theme.
Finishing at 67 Across was...um...jarring.

Cute trick to finish an easy puzzle, completed in less than half my average time.

I love when I open a puzzle, and upon first glance, I can tell the grid is unusual and I’m about to have a good time. I enjoyed all of the scrabble love, but my favorite clue was “hamburger connection?” So witty! I thought the last across clue could have been clued “most powerful” rather than “most valuable” since blanks are worth zero points, but it was all good fun!

Fun Fact: Alfred Butts also designed one other game. Do you know what it was called?

“Alfred’s Other Game” (Yes, seriously).

What was the vertical blue line that kept appearing?? And also my display kept jumping.
I was excited for a moment when I saw the two blanks and wondered whether the letter distribution in the puzzle matched the letter distribution in Scrabble. That would have been amazing. Alas, no.

Disappointingly straightforward for a Thursday, with only a couple of two letter entries including two fairly obvious rebuses qualifying as quirks or gimmicks.  

Nevertheless I appreciated the Scrabble theme.  Both my maternal grandmother and mother were avid (and skilled) Scrabble players, and I fondly remember summer vacations at my grandparents’ house near Lockport, NY and the fiercely contested games the three of us would have.  Despite having only a high school education (and a one room school at that) my grandmother was a killer player. I can’t remember either my mother or me ever beating her, although I came close once or twice.  Seemingly whenever anyone seemed poised to beat her, my grandmother would come up with some arcane word that magically managed to land on enough bonus squares to put the game out of reach.  My mother remained a good player into her nineties, and would take on anyone willing to challenge her at her retirement community, and she rarely lost.  We played at least once a week up until the week before she passed.  My daughter enjoys Scrabble too, although she doesn’t get much chance to play.  I’m hoping my grandson continues the tradition, but I fear his gaming interests will lie in a different area.
Just that little bitty NE corner had me for a couple of minutes. Other than that, another snack puzzle on Thursday.

I really enjoyed this. Lots of fun. 

I’m sure the hate will come. But I liked it

Growing up playing Scrabble in the evenings with my family, I enjoyed this puzzle a lot as a homage to our favorite game, played probably a thousand times over 50+ years (my highest score in a 2-person game: 544, a quantum leap over my second highest score). For a kid, watching my brother and sister and parents fiddle around with their letters for minutes upon minutes, what it taught, beyond vocabulary, was patience, which is not just waiting, but finding ways to occupy my restless mind while waiting my turn. 

Also, in our family, if you put down a word you'd have to have some inkling as to its definition if you were challenged, so we learned not only to spell, but what odd words meant; and if we didn't know, the rule was we could look up the word in M-W (always sitting stolidly in its own place on the table), but only use it in subsequent games. It made it a little more challenging, for me anyway.

It's a feat to use all 100 tiles like Jeff did, with the requisite number of each letter, and to include the blanks, appropriately clued, at the bottom, and I like the broken rule of a two-letter entry at the top. My friend Stan has memorized all the 2-letter words important as glue and point-getters in Scrabble. But Stan had better know what QI means if he's gonna play with my ma*

The easy cluing of this puzzle was off-putting. Thursdays should be harder. But why beat a dead Belmont colt?

So, I said on Tuesday I wasn’t wild about pure tribute puzzles. I really really really don’t care for them on Thursdays. Yeah, maybe there was a little twist at the end but in my opinion too little too late. And as early returns seem to validate, not even a grid or clues that allow for any pushback. I’ll admit I got hung up for just a moment with TREAD before CLEAT, ATPTOUR before WTA, and SAILS before MAILS but other than that it was about as straightforward as possible. C’mon, please guys, you’ve got to give us something more. Anyway, I did post a new Crosshare puzzle today if you still have time on your hands. It’s definitely on the lighter side, more a Wednesday level, but hope it will put a smile on your face. https://crosshare.org/crosswords/XguFVoC0I5CwsEB7Nd36/stock-exchange

A grammar niggle for our esteemed columnist and his copy editor, if any. You wrote:
"Playing the word...descends family game night into a chaos from which it may never recover." 
I'm pretty sure that the game night is the subject of 'descends', not its object. You can descend a staircase, a STEP, or a mountain. You can't descend a game. Of course, the game night can itself descend into chaos. (Ah, memories!) 😌

We have "gifter" and "giftee", "sender" and "sendee", "trainer" and "trainee", etc.  Different entities.

So are "escaper" and "escapee" the same entity?  From the pattern, it seems that the one escaping should be the "escaper", and maybe the prison and its staff is the "escapee"?

Sorry Sean, but the interval between two chromatic notes is a half step. Even if we look at the major scale, it's a half step from mi to fa and from ti to do.

The concept of leaving two squares blank was quite interesting. I find it intriguing when it turns out I don't know some English words - and I don't mean slang, which naturally is often very hard for me to get. Today there were two such words, and they crossed, too, for an additional level of difficulty: HOARY and CLEAT. I've seen the term hoarfrost, which I suppose is related to HOARY, but apparently I never stopped to think what the "hoar" part might mean. I also kind of know CLEAT: as in, I've seen or heard the word, but again, I have obviously never learned what it denoted. The area directly North in the puzzle eluded me the longest because both these words were there.

Perhaps this was accounted for and I simply haven’t updated the app recently enough? But I avoid updating for as long as possible after getting burned with detestable UI changes that can’t be reversed a few times.

Quite a puzzle. Not all that easy for me, of course, and remained 'puzzled' about those last two squares for quite a bit, but finally managed to work it out. And.. an appropriate puzzle find today: A Thursday from December 12, 1996 by J.R. Conrad. The four squares at each corner of the puzzle were... left blank. And the answer across the very center of the puzzle was: _ETY_ Some other theme answers: _TAPE POINT_ _STARE _LOOKS "Fill in..." THE_ Here's that link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=12/12/1996&h=39a ...

If one is going to break the first cardinal rule of puzzlemaking -- i.e. thou shalt not have any two-letter words -- it better be for a really, really good reason or the NYTXW won't publish it.  Right?  So I was waiting for an exceptionally clever puzzle and this certainly didn't seem to be it.  A Scrabble tribute puzzle -- yawn -- with unexceptional fill and unexceptional clues.  But then came the blanks and the belated payoff.  Quite cute.  

I feel sorry for anyone who's never played Scrabble and who doesn't know what blank tiles are.  You won't have any payoff, belated or not.  And without a payoff, this would be one of the most unThursdayish Thursdays ever.

Come to think of it, it's pretty unThursdayish even with a cute payoff.  My tiny second or two of amusement and appreciation at the end didn't compensate for a puzzle I found pretty flat throughout.  I'm betting the constructor felt a real sense of excitement when the blank tiles idea first occurred to him and I wish he could have better sprinkled that excitement around the entire grid.

I do play Scrabble sometimes, but still had trouble with some of these clues. I thought three letters (maybe more?) are worth 10 points (Z, J, Q). So what could be the two most valuable? A worthy Thursday, with a new twist (no rebus).

Whew! I got the rebuses pretty handily but that NE corner was the last to fall for me, with sAILS leaving me grasping at LAs_D_ for a wavelength symbol. Once I asked myself for the Greek L, it landed. I'd have had no hope for getting WTA TOUR any other way.

That North section also had me on the wrong trail with "mock" for made an impression, giving me "oval" for ring... oh boy!

My late aunt and I would play Scrabble often and she would always beat me by a considerable amount. How she managed to always pull the "J", the "Q", and the "Z" tiles always mystified me! Shortly before she passed away, we played our last game, with her grandchildren as observers. I managed to pull the "Z" tile and formed the word "zit". She claimed that "zit" was not a word, much to the chagrin of the kids, who kept saying, "But it is a word!" Finally, she had one of the kids get her Scrabble dictionary, the copyright date of which was 1948!! Needless to say, "zit" wasn't in the dictionary!
On another topic, 42-Across came to me as I was watching a "Big Bang Theory" rerun, when Sheldon mentioned that he had that kind of memory!

This puzzle made me think of another theme idea- the clue number could represent the number of points the word would earn in Scrabble. OAT would be 3, ZA would be 11, etc.

Might be harder to execute with single-digit clue numbers, but I'm sure there's a way to do it. If I had any constructing skill (I do not) I would try it.

@Rich in Atlanta - This reminds me of a search I did 30+ years ago using BLAST -- a genomics and proteomics search engine that revolutionized molecular biology. I did a BLAST search on the amino acid sequence ELVIS and got many results from across all life forms that had AA sequences uploaded. For a comparison, I also ran a BLAST search on the anagram of ELVIS: LIVES. Although I also received some hits, that sequence was far less common in the current proteomes than was ELVIS. Since, at the time, I could come up with no reasonable hypothesis why one sequence of amino acids would be much more common than a sequence of the very same amino acids in a different order, I took this as circumstantial evidence that ELVIS did, indeed, live on in the proteome of all life. Of course, now we know much more about the importance of the order of amino acids in proteins, so this should not, necessarily have been a surprise. However, I more recently performed the same search, and the database of AA sequences is thousands of times larger, and now the frequencies of ELVIS and LIVES are almost equal. I have to conclude that ELVIS has, in the past 30 years, finally reached thermodynamic equilibrium with his surroundings. If anyone wants to confirm this result, they are free to do so -- BLAST still lives! https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi
